newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan lays groundwork for sweeping fiscal reform.
newsitem.headline: Japan lays groundwork for sweeping fiscal reform.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Tuesday laid the groundwork for an overhaul of the nation's debt-ridden finances by setting numerical targets for cuts in a wide range of government spending areas.

In a clear departure from the government's past tradition of merely paying lip service to promises of fiscal reform, Hashimoto proposed cuts backed by numbers even in areas traditionally considered sacred cows.

Hashimoto's cabinet gave approval to a report submitted by a government panel, which called for cuts in key areas such as public works, defence and agricultural assistance with the aim of keeping next year's general expenditures 0.5 percent below this year's levels.

Hashimoto has set fiscal reform as one of his top policy goals and formed the panel in January to live up to his pledge of slashing the government deficit to three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2003.
Japan's fiscal deficit for calendar 1997 is forecast at about 6.3 percent of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels among major industrialised countries.

"The (fiscal) reform carries along with it lots of pain. But it is our responsibility going into the 21st century to overcome the hardships of fiscal reform," Hashimoto told a news conference after the report's release.
Among the sacred cows slated for cuts are official development assistance, to be trimmed by 10 percent next year, and public works, due for a cut of at least seven percent.
The government will now develop an outline for a fiscal reform law by the end of June, incorporating the report's proposed cuts.
It plans to submit the bill to the next extraordinary session of parliament, which is expected to convene in the autumn.
But the fiscal reform plan may not be welcomed whole-heartedly, due to the danger that it may hinder Japan's gradual economic recovery.
The United States is widely believed to be holding such worries, demanding that Tokyo achieve economic growth led by domestic demand.
But Hashimoto brushed aside those concerns, saying: "The fiscal reform plan will bring about an increase in domestic demand over the medium and long term."

Finance Minster Hiroshi Mitsuzuka also said he understands that there will be some deflationary effects from fiscal reforms, but added, "There is no doubt that the base of the economy has become firmer."

Some economists have also pointed out that the reform plan was still far from achieving fiscal "structural reform", saying some of the measures were merely superficial and the plan may end up being a numbers game.

"We must not forget that the real aim of fiscal reform is not just cutting down spending or the state deficit," said Atsushi Miyawaki, a Hokkaido University professor and a member of a group of academics urging overall fiscal reform.
The group urged that priorities on spending should be set according to the effectiveness of a given policy.
There has been criticism that public works projects have strayed from their original purpose and that they have been ineffective.
